FOR CLAT 2027
7

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission

• A high-powered US nuclear ‘executive mission’ will visit India
  from May 17–21, 2026 to assess the country’s nuclear energy
  landscape and identify cooperation opportunities following the
  passage of the SHANTI Act (2025) .

• The mission is organized by the Washington DC-based Nuclear
  Energy Institute (a lobby group of America’s commercial nuclear
  industry) and the US India Strategic Partnership Forum
  (USISPF).

• It will meet with External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar, Power
  Minister Manohar Lal, and Chief Ministers of Andhra Pradesh,
  Maharashtra and Gujarat, and will also hold sessions with the private
  sector in Mumbai.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission

What is Shanti Act? –

• The Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear
  Energy for Transforming India (SHANTI) Act, 2025, was
  passed by Parliament in December 2025 .

• It repeals and replaces the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and
  the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, consolidating
  India’s nuclear legal framework into a single, modern statute.

• It is designed to re-engineer India’s nuclear sector from a state
  monopoly to a regulated, multi-player market.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The 1962 Atomic Energy Act was drafted for an era of autarky and
  kept nuclear power generation the exclusive preserve of the
  government (primarily NPCIL).

• The 2010 Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act created a right
  of operator recourse against suppliers, which foreign companies
  found too risky and deterred investment.

• Over six decades, this framework restricted nuclear power to less
  than 3% of India’s electricity mix, with nuclear contributing
  only 3.1% in 2024-25 and installed capacity of just 8.78 GW.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The new Act explicitly permits private Indian
  companies to build, own and operate nuclear power plants,
  fabricate nuclear fuel, and import/export nuclear fuel – breaking the
  decades-long state monopoly.

• Instead of a uniform ₹1,500 crore cap, the Act introduces graded
  operator liability based on reactor size, ranging from ₹100
  crore to ₹3,000 crore.

• The right of recourse against suppliers is no longer statutory; it
  is now governed by the contract between operator and
  supplier, which makes India’s liability regime more predictable for
  global vendors.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) gets statutory
  status – it no longer functions merely through an executive order,
  enhancing its authority and independence.

• The government retains tight control over fissile materials,
  spent fuel and heavy water, and private entities cannot manage
  sensitive materials .

• A multi-layered compensation mechanism includes the liability cap,
  a government-backed Nuclear Liability Fund, and India’s
  participation in the Convention on Supplementary
  Compensation.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The government’s stated rationale is to provide clean, firm (24×7)
  baseload power that complements renewable energy, which is
  intermittent.

• The target requires scaling up construction from the current small
  reactor programme (220-700 MW) to a fleet-level roll-out, which
  private capital is expected to accelerate.

• SHANTI places a special emphasis on Small Modular Reactors
  (SMRs) as a next-generation technology that is simpler to
  finance and deploy in smaller grids. India aims to
  commission indigenous SMRs by 2033,

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The US-India Agreement for Nuclear Cooperation (commonly
  called the 123 Agreement) was signed in October 2008, enabling
  India to access nuclear exports from the US.

• Implementation was held up for years because of India’s liability
  regime (the 2010 Act).

• With SHANTI removing the statutory recourse-against-suppliers'
  clause, the 123 Agreement can now be operationalized, paving
  the way for projects using Light Water Reactors (LWRs) that
  dominate global nuclear commerce.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• On 29 March 2026, India and the US completed negotiations on
  a reprocessing agreement that grants India the right to
  reprocess US-origin spent nuclear fuel at a dedicated national
  facility.

• This separate arrangement, envisaged in the 123 Agreement, gives
  India the same ability to close the fuel cycle that was previously
  enjoyed only by countries like Japan and Euratom.

• Completion of this reprocessing protocol removes a final
  non-proliferation hurdle and is expected to clear the way for US
  reactor vendors to bid for projects in India.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission

Nuclear Fleet of India –

• India operates 25 nuclear power reactors with a total capacity
  of 8,800 MW.

• The fleet is spread across eight power stations in Tamil Nadu
  (Kudankulam, MAPS), Maharashtra (Tarapur), Rajasthan (RAPS),
  Karnataka (Kaiga), Gujarat (Kakrapar), and Uttar Pradesh (Narora).

• The largest operational reactors are two VVER units at
  Kudankulam (2,000 MW), followed by four PHWR units at Kakrapar
  (1,840 MW) and four at Tarapur (1,400 MW).

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• Rajasthan Atomic Power Station (RAPS) Unit-7 (700
  MW) achieved full-power commercial operation on April 15, 2025,
  becoming India's newest operational large reactor.

• It is part of a batch of sixteen indigenous 700 MW Pressurised
  Heavy Water Reactors being built across the country to expand
  nuclear capacity.

• Its twin unit RAPP-8 is expected soon, and GHAVP-1 & 2 at
  Gorakhpur (Haryana) are also under construction.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• 17 nuclear power reactors with a total capacity of 13,100
  MW are under implementation, including 7 under physical
  construction and 10 under pre-project activities.

• Major reactors under construction include Kudankulam Units 3 & 4
  (2 x 1,000 MW) in Tamil Nadu and two indigenous 700 MW
  PHWRs at Kaiga in Karnataka.

• At Kudankulam, fuel loading for Unit-3 began in early 2025, and
  the unit reached a key commissioning milestone in April 2026.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• Construction of two new 700 MW PHWRs (Kaiga Units 5 and
  6) was approved and officially commenced in February 2026.

• NPCIL awarded the first major civilian contract (nearly ₹12,000
  crore) to a consortium led by Megha Engineering &
  Infrastructure Ltd to build these reactors.

• The project is expected to be completed by 2030-31, significantly
  boosting nuclear capacity in Southern India.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) granted a major
  permit on April 30, 2026, allowing NPCIL to erect major equipment
  at Kudankulam Units 5 and 6.

• The permit covers key components like Reactor Pressure Vessel,
  Steam Generators, and Coolant Pumps for the Russian-designed
  VVER-1000 reactors.

• This decision transitioned the project from civil construction to the
  critical plant installation phase, accelerating progress.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The SHANTI Act establishes a dedicated Nuclear Liability Fund to
  compensate victims in case of a nuclear incident, stepping in when
  damages exceed the operator's liability cap.

• The Nuclear Energy Mission, announced in the Union Budget
  2025-26, provides dedicated policy and financial push to nuclear
  power.

• A total provision of ₹20,000 crore has been made for R&D,
  design, and deployment of Small Modular Reactors
  (SMRs) under this mission.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• Installed nuclear capacity, which was just 4,780 MW in 2014, has
  increased to 8,780 MW (an 84% rise) and is projected to reach
  nearly 22,380 MW by 2031-32.

• The ambitious roadmap beyond 2032 targets: 47 GW by 2037, 67
  GW by 2042, and 100 GW by 2047, 12-fold increase from
  current levels.

• This growth will be driven by completion of large PHWRs, VVERs
  under construction, and a new generation of SMRs.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• India's 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at
  Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu, achieved first criticality on April 6, 2026.

• This milestone makes India only the second country in the
  world after Russia to operate a commercial-scale Fast Breeder
  Reactor.

• The PFBR launches India's second stage of the three-stage
  nuclear programme, enabling utilisation of thorium reserves for
  future power generation.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• India is actively developing three distinct types of SMRs: the 220
  MWe Bharat SMR (BSMR-200) , the 55 MWe SMR-55, and an
  up to 5 MWth High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor
  (HTGR) for hydrogen generation.

• The BSMR-200 and SMR-55 are designed to repurpose retiring coal
  plant sites, while the HTGR is for industrial heat and hydrogen.

• A site for the lead BSMR-200 unit has been proposed at Tarapur,
  Maharashtra.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• Section 3(e) of the SHANTI Act allows ‘any other person’
  permitted by the Central Government through notification, hinting at
  foreign participation without explicitly mentioning FDI.

• Building on the SHANTI Act, the government will soon invite bids for
  a 220 MWe Bharat SMR (BSMR-200), marking a key milestone
  for private participation in the nuclear sector.

• This would be the first time a private Indian company enters the
  operations side of India's nuclear power programme.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission

Recent News –

• The US delegation is led by the Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI),
  the trade association that represents all US nuclear reactor
  manufacturers and fuel suppliers.

• It is co-organized with the US India Strategic Partnership Forum
  (USISPF), a powerful advocacy group that has worked for years to
  remove India’s liability barriers.

• The mission is explicitly designed to “take stock of India’s nuclear
  landscape” after SHANTI and to coordinate US industry
  messaging on the new opportunities.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• The delegation lands in New Delhi on 17 May and stays
  there until 19 May, holding meetings with the Department of
  Atomic Energy (DAE), NPCIL, NITI Aayog, other energy
  ministries and central ministers.

• On 20–21 May, the team moves to Mumbai to meet private sector
  giants: Reliance, Adani Group, Tata Power, JSW Energy,
  Vedanta, L&T, Tata Consulting Engineers and Hindalco.

• US Ambassador Sergio Gor and the US Embassy will set the agenda
  for the formal meetings, which start on the morning of 18 May in
  Delhi.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• One of the most significant features of the mission is the Mumbai
  leg, where the US team will meet more than eight major Indian
  private corporate groups that are not part of the traditional
  public-sector nuclear ecosystem.

• This will mark the first major interface between the US industry
  and India’s private sector after the enactment of SHANTI.

SHANTI Act & US Nuclear Mission


• In April 2026, the US and India announced a separate
  agreement to build six large US nuclear power plants in India,
  giving a concrete shape to the revived cooperation.

• At the same time, India has also been deepening its strategic
  nuclear partnership with Russia: a fresh procurement of five
  additional S-400 units has been cleared, and work on Unit 3 & 4
  of the Kudankulam project (Russian-designed VVER reactors) is
  progressing.

• The government has clearly stated that the technology will be the
  main criterion ─ not the nationality of the supplier ─ as long as the
  liability and safety conditions are met.

The failure of the Delimitation Constitutional Amendment Bill in Parliament in 2026
triggered significant political debate regarding representation, federal balance, and
electoral reforms in India. The proposed legislation aimed to address issues related to
redistribution of parliamentary seats and constituency boundaries based on
demographic changes.

Delimitation refers to the process of redrawing the boundaries of electoral
constituencies to reflect population changes recorded through the Census. The issue
remains politically sensitive because any large-scale redistribution of seats may alter
the balance of representation among states. Southern states, which have experienced
lower population growth rates, have expressed concerns regarding a ________.

Source: The Hindu

Delimitation exercises are generally based on:

A. Tax collection data
B. Population data from Census
C. Number of diverse communities as per Census
D. Voter turnout percentage
ANSWER - B

Delimitation in India is carried out by:

A. Finance Commission
B. Election Commission
C. Delimitation Commission
D. NITI Aayog
ANSWER - C

The freeze on readjustment of Lok Sabha seats was extended through which
Constitutional Amendment?

A. 42nd Amendment
B. 61st Amendment
C. 84th Amendment
D. 97th Amendment
ANSWER - C

Consider the following:

A: Delimitation can alter the number and boundaries of constituencies.

B: Delimitation is unrelated to democratic representation.

A. Only A
B. Only B
C. Both A and B
D. Neither A nor B
ANSWER - A

Why have several southern states expressed concern regarding future
delimitation?

A. Fear of losing legislative and executive powers
B. Concern over reduced parliamentary representation
C. Opposition to Census exercises being conducted with delays
D. Concerns regarding GST allocation
ANSWER - B

In 2026, Indian politics witnessed major developments after Raghav Chadha and
several other Members of Parliament resigned from the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and
joined the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The defections triggered intense debate
regarding political loyalty, party stability, and the effectiveness of India’s anti-defection
framework.

The controversy gained further attention because some of the MPs involved were
members of the Rajya Sabha, the Upper House of Parliament. Questions emerged
regarding whether their actions could attract disqualification under the ______ of the
Constitution, commonly known as the Anti-Defection Law. Political analysts also
discussed the strategic implications for upcoming Rajya Sabha elections and
parliamentary arithmetic.

Source: Indian Express

The Anti-Defection Law in India is contained in:

A. Fifth Schedule
B. Seventh Schedule
C. Tenth Schedule
D. Twelfth Schedule
ANSWER - C

The Anti-Defection Law was introduced through which Constitutional
Amendment?

A. 42nd Amendment
B. 52nd Amendment
C. 61st Amendment
D. 73rd Amendment
ANSWER - B

Questions regarding disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law are decided
by:

A. President of India
B. Election Commission of India
C. Speaker or Chairman
D. Supreme Court directly
ANSWER - C

Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected by:

A. Direct public voting
B. Electoral college of MPs only
C. Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
D. President of India
ANSWER - C

Consider the following:

A: The Anti-Defection Law aims to prevent political defections.

B: Rajya Sabha members have immunity for Anti-Defection Law.

A. Only A
B. Only B
C. Both A and B
D. Neither A nor B
ANSWER - A

The completion of 50 years of Sikkim’s integration into India has renewed focus
on the unique constitutional and political process through which the Himalayan
kingdom became a full-fledged Indian state in 1975. Before statehood, Sikkim
had a special relationship with India under a treaty arrangement that granted
India control over defence, communications, and external affairs.

Political unrest in the early 1970s, demands for democratic reforms, and
tensions involving the monarchy accelerated the integration process. A
referendum was conducted in which a large majority reportedly supported
abolition of the monarchy and integration with India. Parliament subsequently
passed constitutional measures incorporating Sikkim into the Indian Union.

Source: The Tribune

Before becoming a state of India, Sikkim functioned under a special treaty
relationship signed in:

A. 1947
B. 1950
C. 1956
D. 1962
ANSWER - B

Which important corridor connects mainland India to the North-East and lies
close to Sikkim?

A. Rohtang Corridor
B. Wakhan Corridor
C. Siliguri Corridor
D. Ten Degree Channel
ANSWER - C

Which Article of the Constitution contains special provisions relating to Sikkim?

A. Article 370A
B. Article 371F
C. Article 356K
D. Article 368
ANSWER - B

Sikkim became India’s:

A. 18th state
B. 20th state
C. 22nd state
D. 25th state
ANSWER - C

Which of the following best explains why frontier states like Sikkim are
strategically important for India?

A. They regulate India’s monetary system with no tax regime
B. They strengthen border security and regional connectivity
C. They control parliamentary proceedings due to their border sensitivity
D. They determine taxation policy
ANSWER - B

Passage:

The 2026 Assembly elections in West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala attracted
nationwide attention due to their political significance and regional impact. These
states have historically displayed strong regional political identities and have often
resisted direct national political trends.

In West Bengal, the election remained centred around issues such as citizenship
verification, regional identity, political violence, and welfare politics. Tamil Nadu
witnessed intense debates regarding federalism, language policy, social justice, and
relations between the Union and State governments. In Kerala, the contest focused on
welfare governance, secular politics, and economic development, with national parties
attempting to expand their influence.

Source: The Hindu

Which party has been the principal ruling party in West Bengal before the 2026
elections?

A. BJP
B. INC
C. TMC
D. CPI(M)
ANSWER - C

Which issue became a major political theme in Tamil Nadu during the 2026
elections?

A. Low GDP growth year-on-year
B. Three-language policy debate
C. Arctic trade routes
D. Nuclear disarmament
ANSWER - B

Who was the first CM of Tamil Nadu?

A. L.K. Ramanathan
B. M. Karunanidhi
C. J. Jayalalitha
D. C.N. Annadurai
ANSWER - D

In which year was the Partition of Bengal enforced?

A. 1905
B. 1906
C. 1907
D. 1910
ANSWER - A

Passage:

The dispute between Odisha and Chhattisgarh over the Mahanadi River
continues to remain one of India’s major inter-state water conflicts. Odisha has
alleged that upstream projects, barrages, and water diversion structures
constructed in Chhattisgarh may adversely affect downstream water availability,
particularly during non-monsoon months.

The Mahanadi is one of the major east-flowing rivers of peninsular India and
plays a crucial role in irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries, and industry.
The dispute has gained political and legal significance due to concerns
regarding equitable distribution of river waters between upper and lower
riparian states.

Source: The Hindu

The Mahanadi River ultimately drains into the:

A. Arabian Sea
B. Bay of Bengal
C. Indian Ocean
D. Chilika Lake
ANSWER - B

Which major dam is constructed on the Mahanadi River in Odisha?

A. Hirakud Dam
B. Bhakra Dam
C. Tehri Dam
D. Sardar Sarovar Dam
ANSWER - A

In river disputes, the term “upper riparian state” refers to:

A. State located near river mouth
B. State located upstream
C. State with larger population
D. State with coastal access
ANSWER - B

The Mahanadi is classified as a:

A. Himalayan river
B. Glacier-fed river
C. Peninsular river
D. Inland drainage river
ANSWER - C

Which of the following best explains why inter-state river disputes become
politically sensitive in India?

A. Rivers influence judicial appointments due to controversial decisions
B. Water disputes regulate foreign trade
C. Rivers determine parliamentary tenure
D. Water is crucial for agriculture, industry, and drinking supply
ANSWER - D
